note: Real projects at a pinned commit, with answers somebody checked by hand. Run with `npm run corpus`. A number that moves is not automatically a bug - a real fix moves numbers - but it must be re-verified and explained, never recorded blindly. `verified` says how each one was checked; an expectation with no verification behind it is not evidence, it is what the tool said that day.

repos.name: keycloak
repos.why: Red Hat's identity server - the login layer inside banks, insurers and governments. Java, Liquibase and a React admin UI on PatternFly, which is three stacks in one repository.

checks.verified: 2026-10-12. All 77 never-runs read by hand - 31 @Ignore, 21 @Disabled, 19 .skip, 6 confirmed with grep. The single swallows-failure is genuine and is a real defect in Red Hat's admin client: authenticationManagement.spec.ts `try { await getConfig(id); fail('should not find deleted config'); } catch {}` - a bare catch in TypeScript catches everything, including what fail() throws, so the test passes whether or not the config was deleted. It must stay 1 and it must stay that test. Phase 43 shipped 166 here, all the Java expected-exception idiom, which cannot swallow an AssertionError; two more were found and removed in Phase 44, where the empty catch guarded setup and the assertions came after it. unfinished-expectation and tautology are 0 and that is the guard, not an absence.

2026-10-12. 293 findings. The destructive ones were counted independently with grep across the 83 changelogs and match exactly: 67 dropColumn + 39 renameColumn = 106 breaks-old-code, 25 dropTable = destroys-data. filesRead is 89 rather than the 83 changelogs because six real .sql init scripts are read too, correctly reporting nothing. locks-writes was 196 and is 162: the 34 that went were indexes built on tables created in the same changeSet, which hold no rows, and a script confirmed none of the 162 that remain is on a table created in its own file. That suppression existed from Phase 33 and had never worked for Liquibase, because it knew only SQL's CREATE TABLE and not <createTable tableName="...">.

2026-10-12: all 5 barriers opened and read in the source. Two are real defects in Red Hat's production interface - an unlabelled in the account console users see, and a bare in the admin theme editor. The other three are a missing alt and two elements with no lang.

repos.name: openmrs-core
repos.why: A real hospital system. Java and Liquibase, and the second JVM project in the corpus - one sample of a language is not a measurement.

checks.verified: 2026-10-12. 39 never-runs and 1 tautology checked against the source: 37 carry @Disabled or @Ignore directly, VisitValidatorTest has @Disabled after a three-line comment, CreateConceptDictionaryDataSet is disabled at class level, and the tautology is StartModuleAnnotationReuseTest.shouldPass, which is assertTrue(true) and nothing else. swallows-failure is 0, correcting Phase 42, which recorded 2 here as genuine: both are `try { ...; fail(); } catch (Exception e) {}`, which fails properly on the JVM. tautology was 2 until RefByUuidTest was re-read - its assertTrue(true) sits beside a fail() in the catch, so the test can fail. These counts are from after line endings were normalised on read; before that they differed between Windows and Linux. files and tests each dropped by one file on 2026-10-15: OpenMRS ships minified jQuery under webapp/, and one of those files was being judged as a test because minified JavaScript is full of `test(`.

repos.name: bitwarden-server
repos.why: Enterprise password management: the .NET stack that insurance and banking back offices run on. C# with xUnit, 456 EF Core migrations beside 1,264 T-SQL files, and Razor views - three dialects Tewip had never been measured against.

checks.verified: 2026-10-12. 43 never-runs, matching an independent grep for [Fact(Skip= and [Theory(Skip= exactly. swallows-failure is 0 and that is correct rather than missed: bitwarden's test suite contains no empty catch block at all, checked with grep. That is the measurement Phase 43 shipped as an assumption - C# was deliberately excluded from the JVM rule because NUnit, xUnit and MSTest all throw assertion failures deriving from Exception, so catch (Exception) really does swallow them there. If swallows-failure stops being 0, read the new ones. never-runs was 1 before this trial: xUnit's skip attribute was unknown, and the one finding it did have was `collections.Skip(1).ToList()`, which is LINQ.

2026-10-12. 558 findings, down from 919, with 361 false positives removed and every survivor checked. locks-writes was 714: no table was recognised as freshly created, because the pattern read PostgreSQL's "quoted" form but not SQL Server's [dbo].[Grant], and knew no framework's way of saying it - so EF Core's CreateTable followed by CreateIndex, which is what Prisma does, counted every index as blocking writes. All 339 EF Core locks-writes that remain were confirmed by script to be on tables not created in the same migration, and the src/Sql/dbo/Tables definitions now report none at all.

2026-10-12. 251 findings, down from 374. The 111 input-label barriers that went were ASP.NET Core Tag Helpers: asp-for="Name" renders for="Name" on the label and id="Name" on the input, so the association is real and simply not written here. The 3 input-label that remain were opened and read - two labels carrying neither for nor asp-for, and one input whose only description is a placeholder, which is not a label. The link-name findings are genuine: social icon links in the email templates whose only content is an , so a screen reader announces 'link' and nothing else.

repos.name: saleor
repos.why: Commerce, and the largest Python test suite in the corpus. Phase 42 verified it by hand and the numbers then lived only in a commit message.

checks.verified: 2026-10-12. Zero accusations across 12,982 tests - no tautology, no unfinished expectation, no swallowed failure, nothing skipped - and that agrees with the hand verification in Phase 42, which read the condemned list and found it empty. The four zeros are the measurement here: Saleor is the largest Python suite in the corpus and the one most likely to surface a false accusation, so any of them moving off zero needs reading before it is believed.

2026-10-15. 1,433 Django migrations, every one read, none unreadable. 743 findings: 285 RunPython data migrations (slow, which is what they are - application code run against every row inside a migration), 323 RemoveField, 37 DeleteModel, 98 index or constraint builds. locks-writes was 112 until Django's CreateModel was registered as a create form - the only dialect whose create had never been - and the 14 that went are indexes on models created in the same migration, 0055_create_checkout_metadata_model.py among them, which hold no rows and so hold nobody up. All 110 AddIndex/AddConstraint calls in the project name their model, counted independently with grep.

read by hand on 2026-10-18, every finding opened in the file. Saleor's six: four noise (three url-credentials on example.com, which RFC 2606 reserves so it cannot be anybody's system, and one user==password stand-in) and two not-reachable (RSA private keys in test fixtures, conftest.py:149 and tests/settings.py:60, both deliberate). Nothing needs anybody. Before this phase the same checkout reported six needing someone now, at high severity, each told to revoke it at the issuer - three of them the Django postgres://saleor:saleor@localhost default, one on a commented-out line.

repos.name: firefly-iii
repos.why: A real finance application, and the only Laravel project in the corpus. Phase 41 taught `schema` to read its 61 migrations; nothing has held that in place since.

checks.verified: 2026-10-12. 61 migrations read, which is the number Phase 41 established by hand after Laravel was added as a dialect - it had been 0. This entry exists to hold that: Laravel is the only PHP dialect in the corpus, and its rollback is commonly written above the forward path, which is the shape that made it worth testing at all.

2026-10-15. 86 tests, all of them checks, against 88 `public function test*` counted independently with grep - the two missing are in a class that does not extend TestCase. Before Phase 48 this read 95 tests in 39 files with 68 of them 'Tewip would not judge': `$response->assertUnauthorized()` is how a Laravel HTTP test asserts and only `$this->assert` was recognised. Eight of those 39 files were production controllers - testRule, testNotification - endpoints a user hits, not tests; a PHPUnit test is one whose class extends TestCase. One more was a vendored jquery.min.js, which is full of `test(` because that is how a regular expression is applied.

read by hand on 2026-10-18. Zero is the whole point: firefly-iii ships .env.example and .env.testing, which is the classic way a secret scanner embarrasses itself, and the scanner read all of its files and accused none of them.

repos.name: discourse
repos.why: The largest Ruby suite available: 54,846 RSpec tests. Ruby was added in Phase 36 and never measured on real code until Phase 48.

checks.verified: 2026-10-15. 7 never-runs, every one read against its source: 5 `xit` and 2 unconditional `skip`. It was 38 before Phase 48. Thirty were `skip "..." if condition` - a Ruby modifier guard, where the test runs every time the condition is false - and one was an expectation held in a variable and finished on the next line, which RSpec allows and discourse writes. The Go side had refused conditional skips since it was written; Ruby's was added in Phase 36 without it.

2026-10-15. 2,545 Rails migrations, every one read. 1,005 locks-writes confirmed by script to be on tables not created in the same migration; the 61 migrations that use `algorithm: :concurrently` correctly report nothing, which is Tewip recommending the thing discourse already did and then not complaining about it. 550 files were previously reported as migrations Tewip could not read and were library modules, a class, and a locale YAML file sitting under a directory called migrations/.

repos.name: angular-components
repos.why: Angular Material - the Angular team's own component library, with a dedicated accessibility focus. The Angular equivalent of pointing `access` at GOV.UK, and the only Angular in the corpus.

checks.verified: 2026-10-17. 194 barriers, down from 533. The 339 that went were Angular Material's own form fields: <mat-form-field><mat-label>Title</mat-label><input matInput></mat-form-field>, where MatFormField binds the two when it renders - the label is real and simply not expressed in the file. Samples of what remains were read by hand: the ARIA combobox examples carry a placeholder and no label, which is the classic WCAG 3.3.2 failure, and <tr (click)=...> rows really are not focusable. click-without-keyboard was 0 before this trial and is 16: Angular binds events as (click) and Tewip knew four exact spellings, none of them Angular's, so the rule could never fire in any Angular project. mat-checkbox and mat-list-item carrying a click are excluded - they are components that render keyboard-accessible controls.

repos.name: nocodb
repos.why: A real Vue product, and the only Vue in the corpus. 1,132 markup files.

checks.verified: 2026-10-17. 481 barriers, 377 of them click-without-keyboard, which is what a Vue codebase of this age looks like: plain <div @click> with no role, no tabindex and no key handler. Samples read by hand - Breadcrumb.vue's nc-breadcrumb-item is exactly that. It was 286 until Vue's modifier forms were understood: the attribute is @click.stop, not @click, and nocodb has 455 of those.

repos.name: immich
repos.why: SvelteKit, and the only Svelte in the corpus.

checks.verified: 2026-10-17. 25 barriers across 425 SvelteKit files, the lowest rate of the three frontends. Svelte needed no fix at all: both its spellings, on:click and Svelte 5's onclick, were already read, which is why this gap only appeared when a third framework was pointed at.
